Sample.evidence_source: Fifteen older people who had recently made a suicide attempt were interviewed about their experience.

Population.evidence_source: Fifteen older people who had recently made a suicide attempt were interviewed about their experience.

Type.evidence_source: Fifteen older people who had recently made a suicide attempt were interviewed about their experience.

Area.evidence_source: The first research question was concerned with how individuals understand and experience the pathway to their attempt and the second with individuals' subjective experience in relation to various 'risk factors' for suicide and how these factors come together alongside other 'unidentified' factors. Some of the losses and changes that emerged in the pathway to the attempt have been identified elsewhere as risk factors for suicidal behaviour (Cattell, 2000; Draper, 1996). However, what seemed important in the present study was not the mere presence of these 'risk factors', but the way in which they were rendered meaningful by participants, and in particular, the extent to which they experienced them as a turning point and indicative of future decline, dependency and further isolation.The losing control and becoming less visible themes, seemingly cover some of these more 'difficult to define' aspects of attempted suicide that the research to date has failed to address. This helps explain why a risk factor approach to suicide can be limited, and at times misleading.Some of the losses and changes that participants discussed were closely related to the ageing process, whilst others were quite unrelated but were nonetheless experienced within the context of old age, making it difficult to disentangle them from this context. Indeed, although this is not provable, some participants suggested that they may have felt able to manage or better adjust to their difficulties at earlier periods in time. Participants may have been demonstrating difficulties with adjustment to ageing (e.g., Baltes & Baltes, 1990; Brandsta¨dter, 1999), as they persisted with goals that had become unattainable, making it difficult for them to maintain a sense of control over their lives. This coping style has been shown elsewhere to contribute to depression (Brandsta¨dter, Rothermund & Schmitz, 1999). The experience of losing control seemed to tap into a fear of future decline and was strongly linked to negative expectations of old age. This may have made it difficult for participants to maintain a positive focus and create meaning in their lives (Dittman-Kohli, 1990). It is likely that a negative view of growing older contributes to an overall negative attitude towards the future, which has been shown to characterise hopelessness and suicidal thinking prior to an attempt (MacLeod et al., 1993), although few studies have examined this in any detail with older populations (Robin et al., 1977). Many participants felt lonely, detached and generally less socially visible and integrated with others, and feared that this would become worse over time. Failing to draw on social support is commonplace with depression and indeed prior to an attempt (Williams, 1997), and may be even more salient for older adults who either have few opportunities for social contact or find it difficult to utilise those which they have.Williams' (1997) model of suicidal behaviour, in which individuals feel trapped by uncontrollable external circumstances, uncontrollable internal anguish and the impossibility of escape, is useful in understanding experience before the attempt. Some participants construed their decision to act on their suicidal feelings as 'finding a solution'. This fits with Shneidman's (1996) view of a suicide attempt being a drive to seek a solution after reaching a point of feeling entrapped. For other participants, in contrast, the attempt seemed to epitomise their lack of autonomy. These individuals were 'giving up', which was often experienced as another forced choice, adding to feelings of helplessness. In spite of their polarity, the above two conceptualisations of the suicide attempt are linked by the motivation for escape, widely acknowledged as being common to suicidal behaviour (Williams, 1997).Participants' accounts provided an interesting insight into the feelings they faced after they had made an attempt. This is an area that has received little attention in the literature to date, which is surprising given that risk of further suicide is heightened following an attempt. Some participants reported an ongoing desperation and helplessness. Many were still hospitalised at the time of their interview, perhaps indicating that they had not been able to 'move on'. In contrast, other participants felt they had greater control over their lives following the attempt and were perhaps beginning to draw on what Brandsta¨dter (1999) terms accommodative processes. Many participants reported a growing sense of visibility following the attempt, as they felt more socially integrated and more hopeful about the future. This more positive attitude towards the future may serve as a protective factor against future suicidal behaviour (MacLeod et al., 1993). Importantly, the experience of regaining control did not appear to be contingent on time. Some participants described an immediate positive outcome, whilst others interviewed some weeks after their suicide attempt still felt helpless.The fourth research question was concerned with participants' experience of ageing, and whether this impinged upon their suicidal thinking. Some of this has been addressed above within the context of the pathway to and from the attempt. Ageing was also talked about more generally in a negative way and was experienced as a struggle. The stereotypes presented were anchored in strong images of threat, dependency and decline, and closely resembled ageist representations identified in society generally (Featherstone & Hepworth, 1993). In being associated with a group that faces stigma and prejudice from society, it is possible that some participants were negotiating what Goffman (1963) calls a 'spoiled identity', which compounded their depression and suicidal feelings. Many participants felt they had experienced discrimination and negative stereotyping from others on account of their age. Through positioning themselves as being different from other stereotypical older people, using social comparison processes (Heidrich & Ryff, 1993) to think of others worse off than themselves, making distinctions between 'being' and 'feeling' old, and erecting a barrier between the 'young' old and 'old' old participants may have been managing a 'spoiled identity'. Unlike the healthy older participants in Lieberman and Tobin's (1983) study, who talked freely about ageing, some participants were reluctant to think about ageing at all. This might perhaps indicate that they had adjusted less well than some of their peers. The more negative stereotypes of ageing that participants held were often juxtaposed with positive representations, although most participants did not identify strongly with these.The analysis of the interview data reflects the unique interaction between the researcher and participants, rather than some 'objective' truth. As researchers we viewed the data through the lens of our experience as (relatively) younger people, and as clinical psychologists. Therefore alternative interpretations are always possible. Rigorous credibility checks were nonetheless employed to maximise the validity of the findings (Elliott et al., 1999). The interval between the attempt and interview date varied considerably amongst participants, reflecting the difficulty in recruiting from this population. Initially it seemed important to interview participants as close to their suicide attempt as possible so that they could provide fresh accounts of their experience but given that there was no set treatment pattern for older people following an attempt it was necessary to employ a flexible recruitment strategy. Furthermore, there seemed to be no 'correct' time to capture experience with some participants only agreeing to participate in the research once they felt less vulnerable and had 'moved on' from their attempt, whilst others talked about their experience when it was still current. It is possible that some participants' accounts were influenced by the care they received, both formal and informal and they may have withheld information on account of the researcher having to feed back any concerns about risk to their key workers.Within these constraints, however, and given the credibility checks employed in the study, the findings offer a valuable insight into the experience of individuals who attempt suicide in later life, with implications both for future research and for clinical practice. In particular, the study highlights the struggle that many participants encountered before acting on their suicidal thoughts, the nature of experience following the attempt, the extent to which participants felt marginalized and overlooked by others in society because of their age, and the difficulty they had in trying to come to terms with their identity as older people. Indeed, several participants made an explicit link between their difficulty in adjusting to growing older and the motivations for attempting suicide. This merits both further research as it is not widely discussed in the current literature, as well as more consideration in clinical settings so that clinicians are mindful of this transition in their assessments.Not all 'risk factors' identified in the existing literature were present or important to participants prior to their attempt. Other losses and changes were often seen to be more salient, for example individuals' changing status in society on account of their age. This warrants further research and highlights the need for clinicians to focus on the subjective meaning of losses and changes, although this is likely to be an ongoing challenge given the brief length of consultations in general medicine and the unwillingness of some older people to talk about how they feel prior to making an attempt. Participants may have been amenable to individual therapeutic intervention or more community or socially-based interventions (e.g., problem-solving techniques or referrals to day centres) at various 'turning points', which may have served to avert the attempt had the difficulties been recognised and addressed. Where someone has made an attempt, an in-depth interview could be used therapeutically to help identify problems that may hinder recovery or precipitate a repeated attempt. This would go against the idea that talking about suicidal feelings after an attempt can be distressing or can increase vulnerability, neither of which was the case with this sample. Indeed, several participants told their key workers that they valued the opportunity to talk in detail about their experience.
